content: 3. Educational materials should be tailored to the educational level, literacy, and language of each individual and must comply with existing federal, state, and local regulations. 4. 5. Immunizations are an essential component of prevention and infection control programs for DHCP. A comprehensive immunization policy should be implemented in all dental healthcare facilities. 6. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) provides national guidelines for the immunization of healthcare personnel, including DHCP. 7. Dental practice immunization policies should align with current state and federal regulations and recommendations from the U.S. Public Health Service and professional organizations. 8. Healthcare personnel are at substantial risk of acquiring or transmitting vaccine-preventable diseases such as hepatitis B, influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella. ACIP recommends that all healthcare personnel be vaccinated or have documented immunity to these diseases. 9. ACIP does not recommend routine immunization of healthcare personnel against tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis A. No vaccine currently exists for hepatitis C virus (HCV). 10. ACIP guidelines also address immunization recommendations for healthcare personnel with special conditions, such as pregnancy, HIV infection, or diabetes. 11. 12. Some educational institutions and infection control programs provide immunization schedules for students and DHCP. OSHA requires employers to offer hepatitis B vaccination to all employees with potential contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM). 13. Employers must follow CDC recommendations for vaccinations, evaluations, and follow-up procedures. 14. 15. 16. 17. These policies should comply with federal, state, and local requirements. 18. DHCP who have contact with patients may be exposed to individuals with infectious TB. Baseline tuberculin skin testing (TST), preferably using a two-step test, should be conducted at the beginning of employment. 19. The facility's level of TB risk will determine the need for routine follow-up TSTs. 20. DHCP are responsible for monitoring their own health status. Those with acute or chronic medical conditions that increase susceptibility to opportunistic infections should consult their personal physicians or qualified authorities to determine if their condition affects their ability to safely perform their duties. 21. In certain circumstances, healthcare facility managers may need to exclude DHCP from work or patient contact to prevent further transmission of infection. Decisions regarding work restrictions are based on the mode of transmission and the period of infectivity of the disease. 22. Exclusion policies should be written, include a statement of authority defining who can exclude DHCP, and be clearly communicated through education and training. 23. The increased use of latex gloves among healthcare personnel has led to a rise in reports of allergic reactions to natural rubber latex. DHCP should be familiar with the signs and symptoms of latex sensitivity. 24. Diagnosis is made through medical history, physical examination, and diagnostic tests. 25. Procedures should be in place to minimize latex-related health problems among DHCP and patients while protecting them from infectious materials. 26. These records must comply with all applicable state and federal regulations.
